sections.title: Electric Potential Energy: Potential Difference
objectives: Define electric potential and electric potential energy.
Describe the relationship between potential difference and electrical potential energy.
Explain electron volt and its usage in submicroscopic process.
Determine electric potential energy given potential difference and amount of charge.

misconceptions.claim: Potential is the same everywhere around a point charge.
misconceptions.correction: It falls as one over the distance, so it is only equal on a sphere around the charge.

summary: Electric potential is potential energy per unit charge.

The potential difference between points A and B, VB–VA, defined to be the change in potential energy of a charge q moved from A to B, is equal to the change in potential energy divided by the charge, Potential difference is commonly called voltage, represented by the symbol ΔV. Δ V = ΔPE q and ΔPE = qΔV .
An electron volt is the energy given to a fundamental charge accelerated through a potential difference of 1 V. In equation form, 1 eV = 1.60 × 10 –19 C 1 V = 1.60 × 10 –19 C 1 J/C = 1.60 × 10 –19 J.

sections.title: Electric Potential in a Uniform Electric Field
objectives: Describe the relationship between voltage and electric field.
Derive an expression for the electric potential and electric field.
Calculate electric field strength given distance and voltage.
summary: The voltage between points A and B is V AB = Ed E = V AB d (uniform E - field only), where d is the distance from A to B, or the distance between the plates.

In equation form, the general relationship between voltage and electric field is E=–ΔVΔs, where Δs is the distance over which the change in potential, ΔV, takes place. The minus sign tells us that E points in the direction of decreasing potential.) The electric field is said to be the gradient (as in grade or slope) of the electric potential.

sections.title: Electrical Potential Due to a Point Charge
objectives: Explain point charges and express the equation for electric potential of a point charge.
Distinguish between electric potential and electric field.
Determine the electric potential of a point charge given charge and distance.
summary: Electric potential of a point charge is V=kQ/r.

Electric potential is a scalar, and electric field is a vector. Addition of voltages as numbers gives the voltage due to a combination of point charges, whereas addition of individual fields as vectors gives the total electric field.

sections.title: Equipotential Lines
objectives: Explain equipotential lines and equipotential surfaces.

Compare electric field and equipotential lines.

misconceptions.claim: A voltmeter measures the energy of a charge.
misconceptions.correction: It measures the potential difference between two points, and that difference times the charge is the energy.

summary: An equipotential line is a line along which the electric potential is constant.
An equipotential surface is a three-dimensional version of equipotential lines.
Equipotential lines are always perpendicular to electric field lines.

sections.title: Capacitors and Dielectrics
objectives: Describe the action of a capacitor and define capacitance.
Explain parallel plate capacitors and their capacitances.
Discuss the process of increasing the capacitance of a dielectric.
Determine capacitance given charge and voltage.
summary: A capacitor is a device used to store charge.
The amount of charge Q a capacitor can store depends on two major factors—the voltage applied and the capacitor’s physical characteristics, such as its size.
The capacitance C is the amount of charge stored per volt, or C=QV.

sections.title: Capacitors in Series and Parallel
objectives: Derive expressions for total capacitance in series and in parallel.

Calculate the effective capacitance in series and parallel given individual capacitances.
summary: Total capacitance in series 1CS=1C1+1C2+1C3+...
Total capacitance in parallel Cp=C1+C2+C3+...
If a circuit contains a combination of capacitors in series and parallel, identify series and parallel parts, compute their capacitances, and then find the total.

sections.title: Energy Stored in Capacitors
objectives: List some uses of capacitors.
Express in equation form the energy stored in a capacitor.
Explain the function of a defibrillator.
summary: Capacitors are used in a variety of devices, including defibrillators, microelectronics such as calculators, and flash lamps, to supply energy.

The energy stored in a capacitor can be expressed in three ways: Ecap=QV2=CV22=Q22C, where Q is the charge, V is the voltage, and C is the capacitance of the capacitor. The energy is in joules when the charge is in coulombs, voltage is in volts, and capacitance is in farads.

exam_traps.subject: physics
exam_traps.misconception: A voltmeter measures the energy of a charge.
exam_traps.correction: It measures the potential difference between two points, and that difference times the charge is the energy.
exam_traps.signal: Our own teaching of the section, waiting for a paper question that shows the same mistake.

exam_traps.subject: physics
exam_traps.misconception: Potential difference between two points is the force on a unit charge placed between them.
exam_traps.correction: That is the electric field. The potential difference is the work done per unit charge in moving a charge between the two points.
exam_traps.signal: Our own question offers the field definition as an option.

exam_traps.subject: physics
exam_traps.misconception: The potential of a point charge falls with the square of the distance, like the field.
exam_traps.correction: The potential falls as $1/r$. It is the electric field that falls as $1/r^2$, because the field is the gradient of the potential.
exam_traps.signal: Our own question offers the square law as an option.

exam_recall_checks.subject: physics
exam_recall_checks.stem: The potential difference between two points is

options.text: the force per unit charge between them
the work done per unit charge in moving a charge between them
the energy of a charge at the first point

exam_recall_checks.explanation: Potential difference is the work done per unit charge in moving a test charge between the two points.
exam_recall_checks.source: authored against the WAEC physics syllabus

exam_recall_checks.subject: physics
exam_recall_checks.stem: In a uniform electric field, the potential difference between two points a distance $d$ apart along the field is
exam_recall_checks.explanation: The work done per unit charge over a distance $d$ along the field is $Ed$.
exam_recall_checks.source: authored against the WAEC physics syllabus

exam_recall_checks.subject: physics
exam_recall_checks.stem: The potential at a distance $r$ from a point charge $q$ is proportional to
exam_recall_checks.explanation: The potential falls as $V = kq/r$, so it is inversely proportional to the distance. The field, by contrast, falls as $1/r^2$.
exam_recall_checks.source: authored against the WAEC physics syllabus

exam_recall_checks.subject: physics
exam_recall_checks.stem: Two points are on the same equipotential line. The electric field between them is
exam_recall_checks.explanation: The electric field is always perpendicular to an equipotential line, and it is the potential difference along the line that is zero.
exam_recall_checks.source: authored against the JAMB physics syllabus

exam_recall_checks.subject: physics
exam_recall_checks.stem: The energy stored in a capacitor is
exam_recall_checks.explanation: The energy is $U = \frac{Q^2}{2C}$, which is also $\frac{1}{2}CV^2$ and $\frac{1}{2}Q^2/C$.
exam_recall_checks.source: authored against the JAMB physics syllabus
